summary: Describes an experimental Nonce Destination Option used only with ILNP for IPv6 (ILNPv6). It is part of the Identifier-Locator Network Protocol, an experimental, evolutionary enhancement to IP, and comes from the IRTF Routing Research Group.

eli5.summary: A nonce is a random number you attach to a message, like a secret stamp, so the receiver can tell it is a real part of the conversation. It is only an experiment.

questions: what is the ilnpv6 nonce option
how does the nonce protect ilnp sessions
when is the nonce option included in ipv6 packets
subtitle: A secret stamp in IPv6 packets that protects ILNP from off-path attacks.

tldr.problem: When ILNP nodes change locators or send control messages, an off-path attacker could forge packets claiming to be from a valid correspondent, hijacking the session or disrupting communication.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a new IPv6 Destination Option that carries an unpredictable nonce value. Each ILNP session uses a unique nonce, and receivers verify it before accepting control messages or packets from a new locator.
tldr.outcome: The nonce option signals ILNP support and provides lightweight protection against forgeries, enabling backward compatibility and incremental deployment with IPv6.

facts.label: Gratuitous authentication duration
facts.value: At least 3 round-trip times after locator change

today: RFC 6744 is an Experimental Protocol defining a security mechanism used only by ILNPv6 nodes, which have not seen wide internet deployment.

sections.title: Introduction and Purpose
sections.content:
The ILNP Nonce Option is a new IPv6 Destination Option used only with ILNPv6 sessions. It serves two critical functions: First, it signals that ILNPv6 is in use for a network-layer session, distinguishing ILNPv6 from classic IPv6. Second, it provides protection against off-path attacks on ILNP sessions.

Each nonce value is unidirectional, meaning a typical conversation has two different nonces: one from Local Node to Correspondent Node, and a different one in the reverse direction. This limits the number of on-path nodes that can learn an ILNP session's nonce, reducing the risk of session hijacking. The option MUST NOT be used except in ILNPv6 sessions.
sections.eli5: ILNP needs a way to say 'I am using ILNP, not regular IPv6' and to prove that control messages are real. The nonce is like a secret handshake between two nodes that know each other.

sections.title: Option Format and Structure
sections.content:
The Nonce Option is carried within an IPv6 Destination Options header. At most one Nonce Option may exist in a given IPv6 packet. The option includes:

  • Next Header: Identifies the type of header following the Destination Options header.
  • Hdr Ext Len: Length of the Destination Options header in 8-octet units, excluding the first 8 octets.
  • Option Type: 0x8B (139), the assigned value for the Nonce Option.
  • Option Length: Length in octets of the Nonce Value field. Common values are 4 (32-bit nonce) and 12 (96-bit nonce).
  • Nonce Value: An unpredictable, cryptographically random value complying with RFC 4086. Implementations MUST support 32-bit and 96-bit nonces.

The overall option must comply with IPv6 header alignment rules.
sections.eli5: The nonce is just a random number inside a special IPv6 header field. Different nonces are used in different directions between two nodes.

sections.title: Nonce Handling During Mobility
sections.content:
When an ILNPv6 node initiates a session, it generates a unique nonce, stores it in its local ILNP Communication Cache (ILCC), and includes it in its initial packets. A receiver that receives initial packets containing the ILNP Nonce Option learns that the sender supports ILNP and uses ILNP for the session.

When a node's set of valid locators changes (due to mobility or multihoming), the node must send an ICMP Locator Update message containing the Nonce Option with the appropriate nonce value. More critically, the node MUST include the Nonce Option with the correct nonce value in all packets (data or control) to all correspondents for at least three round-trip times after a locator change. This 'gratuitous authentication' ensures that the correspondent accepts packets from the new locators even if the control message arrives late.
sections.eli5: When you start a conversation, you agree on a secret number. If you move to a new address, you keep using that secret number in all your messages for a while so people know it is really you, even if your address changed.

sections.title: Security Properties and Limitations
sections.content:
The ILNP Nonce Option provides non-cryptographic protection against off-path attacks. It is equivalent to the security of ordinary IPv6 sessions that do not use IPsec. For ILNPv6 control messages like ICMP Locator Updates, the received Nonce Option MUST contain the correct nonce value, or the packet is discarded as a forgery.

A receiver must check that nonce values are correct before believing a Locator Update or accepting packets from a new source address. ILNP sessions in higher-risk environments SHOULD also use IP Security (IPsec) for additional cryptographic protection. IPsec use does NOT eliminate the need for the Nonce Option, which MUST still be present and verified.

If the nonce is predictable, an off-path attacker might forge packets. This risk is mitigated by IP Source Address filtering (ingress filtering) and by using cryptographically random nonces.
sections.eli5: The nonce is not perfect cryptography; it just makes it hard for attackers not on the path to forge messages. For really sensitive systems, you should also use stronger encryption.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility and Negotiation
sections.content:
The Nonce Option MUST NOT be present in regular IPv6 packets. When an initiator that supports ILNP wants to establish a session with a responder, it first looks up the responder's DNS records for NID and L64 (or LP) entries. If these are found, the initiator knows the responder supports ILNP and includes the Nonce Option in its initial packets.

If the responder supports ILNP and receives initial packets with the Nonce Option, it uses ILNP for the session. If the responder does not support ILNP and receives packets with the Nonce Option, it MUST drop them and send an ICMP Parameter Problem error message, following normal IPv6 behavior for unknown options.

If the initiator receives no response or an ICMP Parameter Problem error, it infers the responder does not support ILNP and retries using classic IPv6 without the Nonce Option. This negotiation allows ILNP and IPv6 to coexist.
sections.eli5: The nonce option is the secret handshake. If both computers understand it, they use ILNP. If one does not, they fall back to regular IPv6. Nobody is confused.
